newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine analysts worried by lower revs from plan.
newsitem.headline: Argentine analysts worried by lower revs from plan.

text.p: An Argentine congressional committee's decision Wednesday to approve a government austerity plan but unexpectedly maintain the current share of gasoline tax revenues with the provinces could reduce the central administration's expected income, analysts said.
"We certainly did not envision this possibility," said Banco Quilmes economist Pedro Rabasa. "This could reduce the government revenue by around $800 million."
Economist Jose Rutman at Broda consultants said the announcement was "not good news. This was a central element of the package."

Analysts said the market was only mildly pessimistic because of speculation that the government party only agreed to maintain the allocation of tax revenue to speed passage in the Chamber of Deputies. However, they predicted the government will insist on reaping all the tax revenue later in the passage process.

The budget and finance committee of the lower house of Congress decided Wednesday to maintain the system by which income from gasoline is distributed proportionally betweem the central government and the provinces, opposing the government proposal to allow for a larger share of revenue to go to central coffers.
A source from the committee told Reuters the Peronist bloc had adopted that posture to allow the measures to rapidly pass the Chamber of Deputies.

"Since the proportional allocation of the revenue is not changed, that means that we only need a simple majority in the Chamber of Deputies," said the source. "Since we did not have a qualified majority of 130 deputies, this was our best shot."
According to this plan, the measures will then be approved in the Senate where the government has an ample majority and then would have to return to the Chamber of Deputies for revision.
"And at that point we will have something worked out so that we reach the 130-vote majority to pass the package," said the source.
Currently, 29 percent of the tax on gasoline goes to central coffers while the rest goes to the provinces and a fund for subsidized housing largely managed by provinces.

The government had said it expected to boost revenue by $1.6 billion from the increase in gasoline tax in 1997. But if the allocation remains as it currently is, analysts say the government would be getting some $800 million less than requested.
"We should wait a bit and see how this evolves," said economist Aldo Abram at Proeco consultants. "Obviously, if this stays this way it would be a big blow for the government."
